prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: the thalamic mass with early third ventricle compression creates a pressure gradient that risks transtentorial herniation
Do not call the lesion low-grade or demyelinating from its limited enhancement: patchy enhancement is common in diffuse midline glioma, and H3 K27 status from tissue decides.
Do not defer tissue diagnosis on the basis of imaging: H3 K27 status, which defines the entity and its CNS WHO grade 4, can only be established from tissue.
Do not initiate tumor-directed therapy (radiation, chemotherapy) before tissue diagnosis is established
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for MRI-guided stereotactic biopsy of the right thalamic lesion, targeting the posterolateral enhancing component, rather than resection because of the deep thalamic location; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis including H3 K27M and H3K27me3 (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic edema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after the biopsy.
Watch for obstructive hydrocephalus given the third-ventricle compression (worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, papilledema), with urgent CT and neurosurgical CSF diversion if it develops.

Stop the combined oral contraceptive, since estrogen adds to the venous thromboembolism risk of a high-grade glioma and of neurosurgery; offer a copper intrauterine device or a progestogen-only method, and confirm a negative pregnancy test before biopsy and radiotherapy.
Record the sulfonamide allergy: if Pneumocystis prophylaxis is needed (prolonged dexamethasone or chemotherapy), use atovaquone rather than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; the standard for diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered is focal radiotherapy, with a clinical trial where one is available (EANO 2021); temozolomide has no established benefit in this entity.
Discuss prognosis and clinical trial options for H3 K27-altered diffuse midline glioma with the patient and family after tissue confirmation.

Deep lesion; against it: no restricted diffusion (elevated ADC), patchy rather than homogeneous enhancement, immunocompetent host, glial histology

key_clinical_evidence: Diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered, is defined molecularly: WHO CNS5 assigns CNS WHO grade 4 whatever the histology, so a patchily enhancing thalamic lesion should not be called low-grade without H3 K27 status from tissue
Patchy or limited enhancement of an infiltrative thalamic mass is the imaging pitfall of this entity; it does not indicate low-grade biology
Perfusion and spectroscopy localise the most active posterolateral component and target the biopsy, reducing sampling error; they do not grade the tumour

Stereotactic biopsy of a deep thalamic lesion is feasible with high diagnostic yield and is the only route to H3 K27 status; the deep location is a reason for biopsy rather than resection, not a contraindication to tissue
Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with third-ventricle compression and early ventricular enlargement; CSF is also low-yield for a primary brain tumour
The prior visual episode with a non-specific white matter lesion could anchor toward demyelination, but an expansile infiltrative thalamic mass progressing over weeks requires tissue

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 30-year-old right-handed graduate student who presents to the neurology inpatient service following evaluation in the emergency department for three weeks of progressive headaches and newly recognized left-sided weakness. She reports that approximately three weeks ago she began experiencing persistent, dull, bifrontal headaches that were initially attributed to dissertation-related stress. Over the following week, the headaches worsened and began to wake her from sleep in the early morning hours, which she found unusual. She took over-the-counter ibuprofen and acetaminophen with only partial and transient relief. Approximately two weeks ago, she noticed that her left hand felt clumsy — she was dropping items and had difficulty typing accurately, which she attributed to fatigue. Within days, she recognized that her left leg also felt slightly weak and heavy when walking. Concurrently, she began experiencing intermittent episodes of double vision, predominantly on left lateral gaze, lasting seconds to a minute, occurring 3-5 times daily over the past 5 days. She denies any seizure activity, loss of consciousness, focal numbness, or sensory loss, though on careful questioning she acknowledges that the left side of her body feels slightly less sharp to pinprick. She denies fever, night sweats, or recent infections. She has no bowel or bladder dysfunction. Her primary care physician evaluated her two weeks ago and attributed the headaches and fatigue to iron-deficiency anemia and restarted ferrous sulfate; a complete blood count at that time was notable for a hemoglobin of 11.4 g/dL. She was referred to neurology when her weakness progressed. Notably, she had an episode of transient visual blurring in the right eye three years ago that resolved spontaneously over two weeks; MRI at that time showed a small white matter lesion, but no demyelinating diagnosis was established and she was not followed up. She is anxious about the current symptoms given her family history — a maternal uncle died of a brain tumor in his late 40s.
